en: With black eyes like twin morning stars,
Shed tears from those dark eyes,
Grieving truly, beating her breast,
And came pleading to Seytek,
The hero born in truth.
Clutching his bridle, she screamed,
That wretched, afflicted woman,
Answering with sobs and bitter weeping.
Tormented by sorrow,
She grasped the young man's bridle
And cried aloud in supplication:
“O river valley, my flowing spring,
My young hero found when death was near,
My banner borne upon the spear,
While I remained behind in Altai,
My keepsake left by a noble man!
My deep-rooted sacred plane tree,
Whose sight lifts the gloom from my brow,
My steadfast poplar and plane tree,
From the gray-maned hero gone to the next world,
You are the breath left to sustain me.
My very breath, I have words for you:
You are going to your land,
To Jylgyn, broad Keng-Kol, and spacious Talas.
You are going to your people,
The joyful Kyrgyz and the few Argyn.
Is there a raging Chinese enemy
That requires us both to go together?
Is there some dispute to argue,
Sweating brow and wearing out the tongue?
Alas, brother, what are you saying?
Who could listen to these words of yours?
Let only a dark night hear them,
Let the dug grave hear them,
Let the dark earth hiding all things hear them—
Who else could bear to hear?
‘I shall go alone to my land,
I myself shall go to my people,’”
So spoke brave Seytek,
While Külchoro, born of noble stock—
Külchoro remained behind and halted.
Now look as he wheeled about,
His eyes reddening into embers,
Poised like a striking serpent,
Preparing like a seasoned warrior,
Wisdom coming to him as if from the unseen,
He readied himself in wrath,
And girded on a sword without a sheath.
At the sight, every heart was stirred;
He seemed a towering blue mountain,
A dark ridge above surging waves,
A lion of surpassing majesty,
A hero perfect in his might.
He thundered, spreading dread,
And every mortal who beheld him
Felt his whole body shudder.
Such was Seytek’s state:
Waking in urgent haste,
The valiant man, like Surayyl,
Crouched like a gray tiger ready to spring.
He hurriedly performed his devotions,
Saddled his dark bay horse,
Prepared all his arms and gear,
And girded on his naked sword.
He was the image of his forefathers—
Behold his lionhearted courage!
When wicked men unleashed disaster,
Your father’s blood-red Akolpok,
Armor fitted for your lionhearted father,
Those six vile ones who had grown up among us
Put it on in this manner,
And wore it after defiling it,
Then scoured the face of the earth.
They dressed him in a Jekeyboz coat,
Mounted him on the swift Jelmaian,
And lavished livestock along the way,
Sending men through many cities,
Making camels kneel in every place,
Seeking fine cloth from city to city.
They searched the city of Bombay
And paid gold to obtain
The cloth of Bakburchun,
Mending all that was damaged,
Repairing all that was chipped.
Whatever proved unfit was broken apart,
Steel was filed and fitted
Into the spaces between.
With awls made of steel,
Bent and shattered by the work—
“Almighty God of power,
A grievous calamity has come,”
Karimbay wept when he saw it.
The women twisted the backing threads,
And champions among all living men,
Warriors, examined and tested it.
They repaired its woven backing;
My noble mother Kanykey,
Sleeping not at night,
Resting not by day,
Your suffering grandmother restored it.
She strengthened its backing with gold,
While sixty women and widowed sisters-in-law
Grew weary and exhausted by the task.
Its links were fine as a hen’s eye,
Its rings flickered like a lark’s eye,
So tight that a needle’s point could not enter.
Ten patterned saddlebags and ten carpets—
I know the customs of the Ogoy.
Forty embroidered saddlebags and forty carpets—
My child, I know the customs of the Kyrgyz.
Our Talas is a precious land:
Deer bellow in its rugged hills,
Cuckoos call from its sunny slopes,
Its flowers laugh in crimson bloom,
Though my darling knows me not.
Its springs surge and overflow,
Its nightingales sing sweetly—
Such is our land of Talas.
There they sow autumn rice,
Cuckoos sing among the willows,
Wild asses gather on the plains,
And argali graze upon the hills—
Such is our famed land of Talas.
My young hero found when death was near,
When you go to your people, be content;
Go safely and return unharmed,
Come swiftly and do not leave me longing.
If you meet your grandsire Bakai,
Rescue him from his grief!
Your true enemy is Kanchoro;
Go to Kanchoro, who now rules as khan.
Ask him to return as your inheritance
The countless treasures left by your father!
If he confronts you and refuses your words,
If he will not give you your inheritance,
Return without trading insults,
And come tell wretched me,
“Mother, he refused to give it!”
When they ravaged my people,
When yesterday those villains wrought evil,
When they plunged us into torment,
When they slaughtered the heroes,
When they slew my blessed protector,
When they massacred so many of mine,
When they destroyed my shelter,
Those quarrelsome, accursed kinsmen—
Do not by chance trade insults with them.
Coax and flatter them,
Using your honeyed tongue.
From the hands of that rabid dog,
Recover the Akolpok armor.
If he should suddenly act perversely,
If by chance he refuses to give it,
Come and tell wretched me,
“Mother, he refused to give it,”
Then return and let me contend
With that black-hearted dog.
The great inheritance left by your forefather
Brought on a mighty upheaval;
A heavy musket fell across my neck,
And blood was spilled into my bosom.
Great anguish came upon us;
We struggled like wolves,
Our coal-black hair
Streaming as we staggered along.
Our berry-patterned dresses
Were ripped apart at every fold,
While murderous blood poured in streams.
We screamed and tore our hair,
Our frail lives scattering like flies.
They were an army; we were alone.
When they came against us by force,
We wailed and wept in grief,
And lost your father’s Akkelte—
We were parted from Akkelte.
If you ask what Akkelte is like:
When aimed at an attacking foe,
It fires of its own accord;
The hostile enemy who faces it
Is plunged into torment,
And the doomed foe is struck down.
When the moment comes,
A bullet flies from its muzzle as it is raised.
Enemies struck by its bullet
Fall with a thud before the smoke appears;
Once its shot reaches them, they are gone.
Akkelte’s bullet could not pierce that armor,
Nor could the point of a spear,
Embers of burning hardwood could not scorch it,
Nor bullets from a heavy gun penetrate it.
Its collar is gold, its sleeves are brass,
True chain mail with rings like larks’ eyes,
Half a yard in thickness.
When they surrounded the stronghold,
Bringing ruinous calamity and great strife,
When those mangy dogs attacked,
Plundering all our possessions,
And looting the royal camp,
I, your mother, was seized first,
My black hair hanging loose,
My face torn and bleeding.
I fainted, my spirit extinguished,
With no son to be my champion.
When my fate turned utterly cruel,
The senseless infidel Kanchoro
Struck your mother to the ground.
My strength failed and left me,
Black blood streamed from my side;
I, your ill-fated mother,
Had every part of my body
Beaten dusty by the lash.
Your moon-faced mother’s fair countenance
Was bloodied by five clawing nails.
The treasured saddlebag upon my back
Was carried off as plunder,
And Akolpok remained behind
In the hands of the slave Kanchoro.
If you wear it, no bullet can pierce it;
It is the armor to wear into gunfire.
Go and see the field where I was disgraced,
And learn what befell your mother.
Coax and flatter him,
And from that wretched slave’s hands
Bring Akolpok back and wear it.
If by chance he refuses to give it,
Then take up against that stubborn swine
The radiant weapon, when raised,
The exiled warrior’s bright treasure—
Akkelte, which fires afar,
The solace of this mortal life.
Such is the nature of Akkelte.
Almabash is a matchless steed,
Heeds neither distance nor nearness,
And carries you far whenever you mount.
If he sweeps past the hostile foe,
They lose their wits and scatter.
Its sights were mounted in gold,
And those who heard its report fell dead.
Whoever came within its path crawled away;
No other short gun ever matched it,
And none who challenged it prospered.
When the holy man in Kokand
Was crying out in distress,
While suffering humiliation,
When crooked rebels raised strife,
Your grandfather, lion of the world,
Was setting matters right,
And cherished and tended
The black-steel Zulpukor,
Keeping it always ready,
In those days when he spread
Great alarm throughout the world—
Your gray-maned grandfather went
To a settlement beyond Almak,
And from a Russian hauling a cart
He seized the gun after coveting it.
